name: args (Taywee)
workload: 100,000 iterations of constructing a parser and parsing the 13-token command line '-i 7 -c a 2.7 --char b 8.4 -c c 8.8 --char d' (one int flag, a char list flag, a positional list of doubles), with asserts on the parsed values.
claimed_speedup: README 'How fast is it?': 'about 65% faster than TCLAP and 220% faster than boost::program_options'. Run output in the README: args 0.895472 s, tclap 1.45001 s, boost::program_options 1.98972 s. Ratios derived from page data: boost::program_options takes about 2.22x as long as args, TCLAP about 1.62x as long.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -obench bench.cxx -O2 -std=c++11 -lboost_program_options (compiler version and Boost version not stated)
tradeoffs: Single-header C++11 library, MIT. Python-argparse-like API with static typing, nestable group logic, help generation and bash completion. UTF-8 support is limited (no normalization). The author calls it feature-complete: bug fixes only, no new major functionality.
caveats: First-party micro-benchmark whose full source is printed in the README, but no CPU model, compiler version, Boost version or date is given, so it cannot reach tier A. Each iteration times building the parser object plus one parse of a 13-token line, about 9 microseconds per iteration for args, which is irrelevant for a CLI that parses once per process. The author says the command line was trimmed to what TCLAP could handle. The README percentage wording is loose: the stated '220% faster' than boost::program_options matches a time ratio of about 2.2x (about 122% higher throughput), and '65% faster' than TCLAP is about 62% by time ratio (derived from page data). Nothing compares against getopt. The Boost loop passes the original argument vector and never calls po::notify, so it does slightly less than a full Boost.Program_options use. Numbers are undated and probably from an old Boost release.

name: cofetch
workload: 20,000 HTTP GETs against a local nginx (keep-alive) with 100 requests in flight: one cofetch thread against one-request-at-a-time synchronous cpr and cpp-httplib clients; also 20 threads per client, 10 ms and 50 ms injected RTT, and a 2,000-request dependent chain.
claimed_speedup: README: '+35% single-thread throughput over the fastest sync client, +31% with one event loop per core against equal-sized thread pools, +16% on sequential chains driven from a busy-poll loop'. bench/README.md one-thread table: cofetch 18,240 req/s (busy poll) and 17,412 req/s (run()) vs cpp-httplib 12,889 req/s and cpr 10,127 req/s; 20 threads: cofetch 166,646 req/s vs cpp-httplib 127,333 and cpr 122,122; chain: cofetch busy-poll 14,804 req/s vs cpp-httplib 12,761 and cpr 10,209; at 10 ms RTT one cofetch thread (9,353 req/s) ties 100-thread pools (cpp-httplib 9,571, cpr 9,345) and runs about 98x ahead of a single-threaded sync client (stated on the page).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 14 -O3, Release CMake build, libcurl 8.14, asio 1.38, Debian 13 on WSL2; bench/run_bench.sh builds and runs everything
hardware: WSL2 host with 20 logical cores (CPU model not stated); run-to-run variance about +/-10% per the page
tradeoffs: Header-only (needs libcurl and ASIO), C++17, C++20 coroutines optional; callbacks, futures and coroutines from one implementation; libcurl gives HTTP/2, TLS and connection pooling. Needs an asio::io_context to drive it. Very new repo (first commit 2026-07-10).
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code (bench/) but the CPU model is not stated, so tier C. The headline is asynchronous (100 requests in flight on one thread) against synchronous clients with one request in flight, so the single-thread win measures concurrency, not a faster HTTP client; with 10 ms RTT it only ties a 100-thread pool. In the sequential chain the README uses the busy-poll mode: in the default run() mode cofetch (11,116 req/s) and its coroutine form (10,547 req/s) are slower than cpp-httplib (12,761 req/s), and the page says so. Loopback to local nginx on WSL2, not a real network. Compared to cpr both sit on libcurl. The page also reports an internal epoll baseline about 14% faster than cofetch on loopback.
